extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, critics, and readers interested in literary taste and composition
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical maxims about writing, revision, taste, and the practice of criticism aimed at producing durable and graceful literature. Includes guidance for pupils, cautions about topicality and affectation, and remarks on the critic's habits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer general principles for longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: He that writes upon general principles, or delivers universal truths, may hope to be often read, because his work will be equally useful at all times and in every country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want a work to endure, aim for universal truths rather than transient topics; 'that which is to be loved long, must be loved with reason rather than with passion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical writing gains readers quickly but fades
rubrics_metrics.description: He that lays his labours out upon temporary subjects, easily finds readers, and quickly loses them; the effect ceases with its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use topical allusions and current events when you need immediate attention, but expect such works to decline rapidly in interest once circumstances change; weigh immediacy against longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The art of blotting (revision by subtraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The great art is the art of blotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision should emphasize pruning and deletion as essential to good writing; removing excess often improves clarity and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid slavish adherence to arbitrary rules (e.g., 'keep nine years')
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule that 'every piece should be kept nine years' is presented as a critic's aphorism rather than an absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of dogmatic, one-size-fits-all prescriptions offered by critics; evaluate rules in context rather than following them blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy nature: favour naturalness in art
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief business of art is to copy nature; devoted attention to nature should inform good writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek fidelity to natural human behaviour, feeling, and speech in character and scene; avoid affectation that departs from believable nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain tonal and formal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms are made of mixing comic with tragic scenes or of part-blank, part-rhymed plays as 'absurd'; such mixtures disrupt natural course of passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jarring blends of tone or inconsistent versification within a single work unless you have a deliberate, controlling design for the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of versification sustains interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's 'perpetual variation of the numbers' gratifies the ear and awakens attention; even rugged lines temper melodious luxury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poetry, vary cadence and rhythm to maintain reader/listener engagement; deliberate roughness or cadence shifts can serve expressive purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational truth secures lasting value
rubrics_metrics.description: So vainly is wit lavished upon fugitive topicks; so little can architecture secure duration when the ground is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the underlying truth or soundness of your subject and argument; elegant expression on a false or unstable foundation will not endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless scrupulosity and affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: The graces and subtilties of composition are laudable while they increase pleasure, but easy to be refined by needless scrupulosity till they shall more embarrass the writer than assist the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let excessive refinement turn into affectation; clarity and genuine pleasure for the reader should trump showy niceties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read the best authors; imitate beauties, avoid faults
rubrics_metrics.description: The pupil is advised 'to read none but the best authors; and when he finds one congenial to his own mind, to study his beauties, but avoid his faults.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model yourself on exemplary writers, consciously emulating strengths while being alert to their failings; choose influences that fit your own genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overload the mind with contrary studies
rubrics_metrics.description: He enjoins him, with great earnestness, not to read more than he can digest, and not to confuse his mind by pursuing studies of contrary tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the quantity and heterogeneity of reading/study so it can be assimilated; avoid mixing incompatible modes or disciplines that fragment style and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work when imagination and judgment coincide, but keep within nature
rubrics_metrics.description: He exhorts him to catch those moments when he finds his thoughts expanded and his genius exalted, but to take care lest imagination hurry him beyond the bounds of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in moments of inspiration, but temper flights of imagination with plausibility and coherence; do not let enthusiasm override naturalness and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and cultivate your particular genius
rubrics_metrics.description: He tells him, that every man has his genius, and that Cicero could never be a poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the kind of writing that suits your abilities and temperament; do not force yourself into incompatible modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of critics' easy malignity and vague epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism often supplies 'the want of meaning with words' and uses convenient epithets—'manly', 'dry', 'stiff', 'flimsy'—applied to books not read or not understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing work, anticipate superficial judgments; when evaluating, avoid lazy terminology—be specific rather than resort to stock labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish despite excessive scrupulosity; life is short
rubrics_metrics.description: Many leave labours unfinished because they prescribe to themselves such a degree of exactness as human diligence can scarcely attain; life is short, knowledge endless, and many doubts deserve not to be cleared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist perfectionism that prevents completion and publication; accept that some uncertainty and imperfection are inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness about contemporaries may demand delay
rubrics_metrics.description: He that writes the history of his own times, if he adheres steadily to truth, will write that which his own times will not easily endure; he must be content to reposite his book, till all private passions shall cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your truthful account will inflame present passions or cause harm, consider postponing publication until controversy subsides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious of institutions or tribunals of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Minim's plan for an academy of criticism would 'authoritatively direct the theatres' and impose 'the nicest rules'—presented as an overreaching desire of critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism about centralized, prescriptive taste-making: formal tribunals or academies risk suppressing diversity and imposing narrow standards; value plural judgment and individual taste.
